parole.significato: to air (bring something into contact with the air), aerate, air out
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek αερίζω (aerízo). Compare Aromanian airisescu, airisiri.
Borrowed from Greek αφιέρωσα (afiérosa), aorist of αφιερώνω (afieróno).

Probably from Greek μάλαμα (málama, “gold”), compare Aromanian malamã (“gold”), Megleno-Romanian amálomă (“gold”), Albanian malamë (“gold”). The loss of the initial m can be attributed to influence from aramă (“copper”). Compare also Italian lama (“metal plate”), Serbo-Croatian lama, lim.
Borrowed from Greek άλλα άντ’ άλλα (álla ánt’ álla).

parole.significato: decorative chain, such as that of a pocket watch
robes died with Tyrian purple, imperial purple, royal purple

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek ὰναλογία (ánalogía). Doublet of analogie.
Borrowed from Greek ανθρωπολατρεία (anthropolatreía). By surface analysis, antropo- + -latrie.
Borrowed from Greek απορία (aporía) or French aporie.

parole.significato: stake (used as a prop in vineyards, or for other hanging plants)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek ἐργαλεῖον (ergaleíon). First attested in 1816.

parole.significato: guestmaster, monk who receives guests in the monastery

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek Αρβανίτης (Arvanítis). Doublet of arnăut.
Borrowed from Greek αρραβώνας (arravónas), inherited from Ancient Greek ἀρραβών (arrhabṓn), itself borrowed from Biblical Hebrew עֵרָבוֹן (ʕerɔḇon).

parole.significato: bud (newly formed leaf or flower that has not yet unfolded)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek μπατάλια (batália), from Italian battaglia, itself from Late Latin battualia, and thus doublet of bătaie, which was inherited from Latin.
Borrowed from Greek καμπύλεισα (kampýleisa). First attested in 1879.
Borrowed from Greek καλαπόδι (kalapódi), from Ancient Greek καλοπόδιον (kalopódion). Doublet of calibru.
Borrowed from Greek καρφίτσα (karfítsa). Compare Aromanian cãrfitsã.
Feminine of castan, from Greek κάστανα (kástana).
Borrowed from Greek καταδέχομαι (katadéchomai). Cognate to Aromanian cãtãndisescu (“to end up”).

parole.significato: wall in front of the altar

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek κατηγορία (katigoría). Doublet of categorie.
Borrowed from Greek κέφαλος (kéfalos), from Ancient Greek κέφαλος (képhalos, “head”).

parole.significato: an elegant and frivolous young lady
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek κερατσιτσα (keratsitsa), from κεράτσα (kerátsa), variant of κυράτσα (kyrátsa), from Ancient Greek κυρά (kurá, “lady”).
Borrowed from Greek κύκλος (kýklos). First attested in 1773.
Borrowed from Greek κουφέτα (kouféta), from Italian confetto.
Borrowed from Greek καλτσούνι (kaltsoúni), from Italian calzoni (“trousers, pants”), but itself an augmentative of calza (“sock, stocking”).
Borrowed from Greek χορός (chorós, “dance”), or borrowed from Latin chorus, Italian coro, German Chor. Doublet of horă.
Borrowed from Greek κόρτη (kórti), ultimately from Latin cors or cohors. Doublet of the inherited curte, as well as the later borrowing cohortă.
16th century borrowing from Greek κούκουρον (koúkouron) (cf. also Albanian kukur), from Latin cucurum or Byzantine Greek κούκουρον (koúkouron), possibly ultimately of Hunnic or Mongolic origin.

Often considered to be from Greek κουκουβάγια (koukouvágia), but seems linked to a number of foreign cognates, including Albanian kukuvajkë, Italian coccoveggia, cuccumeggia, Calabrian cucumau, cuccuvella, Sardinian cuccumeu ~ cuccumiau, and Sicilian cuccuvìu. Other theories include a Vulgar Latin *
Borrowed from Greek κούπα (koúpa), ultimately the same as Etymology 1.
Back-formation from curmale, plural of an earlier form *curma, from Greek χουρμάς (chourmás), from Ottoman Turkish خرما (hurma), from Classical Persian خُرْمَا (xurmā).
Borrowed from Greek καλαμάρι (kalamári). Doublet of calmar.
Borrowed from Greek or Byzantine Greek καλόγερος (kalógeros), possibly partly though a Slavic intermediary; compare Serbo-Croatian kaluđer, Bulgarian калугер (kaluger). Cf. also Aromanian cãlugãr.

Most likely borrowed from Greek κάμαρα (kámara), from Latin camara (variant of camera), itself from Ancient Greek κᾰμᾰ́ρᾱ (kămắrā). An etymology straight from Latin or a Vulgar Latin form is unlikely. Compare Aromanian cãmarã, Albanian kamëre, Turkish kemer, Bulgarian камара (kamara). Doublet of cam

parole.significato: a mythical dog-headed monster or ogre
parole.testo: Unknown. Generally believed to be based on a calque of Greek κυνοκέφαλος (kynokéfalos, literally “dog-head”). (See cap and câine, cf. Aromanian capdicãne). The -un suffix may indicate an expressive treatment, similar to gărgăun. Also, possibly from a Medieval Latin *capcanus, or linked with an old T

parole.significato: a 19th century progressive in Wallachia and Moldavia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek καρβουνάρης (karvounáris), from Italian carbonaro.
Borrowed from Greek δίπλα (dípla) or Serbo-Croatian diple.

parole.significato: administrator of the finances of a monastery
dish (flat round object), especially one used in church services to collect money
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek δίσκος (dískos), partly through a Slavic intermediate.

parole.significato: a group of twelve boyars from the retinue of the prince

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek δράμι (drámi), from Byzantine Greek δράμι (drámi), from Arabic دِرْهَم (dirham), from Middle Persian 𐭦𐭥𐭦𐭭 (ZWZN /⁠drahm⁠/), from Ancient Greek δραχμή f (drakhmḗ, “drachma”).
Borrowed from Greek δάδα (dáda), influenced by words like duducă, neneacă, babacă, etc.

parole.significato: in Orthodox liturgy, a part of a prayer that is uttered aloud and clearly

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek οικονόμησα (oikonómisa), aorist of οικονομώ (oikonomó).

parole.significato: a prayer uttered by the priest during the sermon

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek Έλληνας (Éllinas), from Ancient Greek Ἕλλην (Héllēn).
Borrowed from Greek Εγγλέζος (Englézos), from Byzantine Greek Ἀγγλέζος (Anglézos), from Italian inglese.
Borrowed from Greek ενορία (enoría) (18th century). Compare Aromanian enurii.
Borrowed from Greek ἐνθουσιαστικός (enthousiastikós). By surface analysis, entuziast + -ic.

parole.significato: diocese or bishopric in the Orthodox Church; eparchy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek επαρχία (eparchía), from Ancient Greek ἐπαρχία (eparkhía). By surface analysis, eparh + -ie.
Borrowed from Greek ἐπιμελέομαι (epimeléomai). First attested in 1797.

Borrowed from Greek επίσκοπος (epískopos), from Byzantine Greek, from Ancient Greek ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos) (perhaps partly borrowed through Latin episcopus or Old Church Slavonic епискоупъ (episkupŭ)). Cf. also the archaic or regional doublet piscup.
Borrowed from Greek επισκοπία (episkopía). Equivalent to episcop + -ie.

parole.significato: guardian (person legally responsible for a minor)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek αἱρετοκρισία (airetokrisía). First attested in 1775.
Borrowed from Greek φάκλα (fákla) or Bulgarian факла (fakla), ultimately from Latin facula (thus a doublet of fachie, făclie, and flacără).
Borrowed from Greek φασόλι (fasóli). Compare Italian fagiolo.

parole.significato: wedge, slice, piece cut off from the rest (usually said of food)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek φελλί (fellí), from Late Latin offella. Compare Aromanian filii, filie, fãlii, and Sicilian feḍḍa.
Borrowed from Greek θυρίδα (thyrída). Compare Bulgarian фирида (firida), Aromanian firidã.
Borrowed from Greek φίσα (físa), from French fiche. Doublet of fișă.

Probably from Greek φλάμμουρος (flámmouros). Was thought to be from Latin flammula, diminutive of flamma, but it is less likely that it was an inherited or popular word. Compare also the Albanian cognate flamur and Aromanian flãmburã, which probably come from the same Greek source.
From folos, from Greek όφελος (ófelos). Compare also Aromanian felisescu.

parole.significato: fried bread with milk and eggs

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek φούστα (foústa), from φουστάνι (foustáni), from Italian fustagni.
Borrowed from Greek γαλιόνι (galióni) or French galion or Italian galeone.
Borrowed from Greek γουβίδι (gouvídi), itself a diminutive form ultimately derived from Ancient Greek κωβιός (kōbiós) (cf. also Latin gobius).
Borrowed from Greek άμπακας (ámpakas). First attested in 1779.
Borrowed from Greek χάρτης (chártis). Doublet of hârtie, carte, and cartă.
Borrowed from Greek ιεροδιάκονος (ierodiákonos). First attested in 1766.
Probably from Greek χώμα (chóma), possibly partially through a Bulgarian хума (huma). Compare Aromanian umã, which may be linked directly to Latin humus.
Borrowed from Greek ηγεμονικός (igemonikós). Doublet of hegemonic.

parole.significato: mold or mildew grown on inner walls inside a house

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek ύψιλον (ýpsilon), from Ancient Greek ὖ ψῑλόν (û psīlón). .

parole.significato: synonym of istorisi (“to recount a story”)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek ιστόρησα (istórisa), aorist of ιστορώ (istoró), from Ancient Greek ἱστορέω (historéō), from ἵστωρ (hístōr).
Borrowed from Greek δυόσμος (dyósmos, “mint”), ultimately from Ancient Greek ἡδύοσμον (hēdúosmon, “green mint”).
Borrowed from Greek λαβράκι (lavráki), from Ancient Greek λάβραξ (lábrax).

parole.significato: a monk living in a laura

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek λεύτερος (léfteros, “free”), from Ancient Greek ἐλεύθερος (eleútheros).
Borrowed from Greek ληθαργικος (lithargikos). By surface analysis, letargic + -esc or letargie + -icesc.
Borrowed from Greek λείψω (leípso), future of λείπω (leípo, “I am absent, leave, lack”).
Borrowed from Greek λοκάντα (lokánta), from Italian locanda, from Latin locanda, from locandus.

Borrowed from Greek λεμόνι (lemóni), ultimately from Persian لیمو. Though the borrowing must be over 500 years old to have undergone numerous Romanian-specific phonological changes already present in the earliest of Romanian texts.
Borrowed from Greek λεχούσα (lechoúsa), variant of λεχώνα (lechóna).

parole.significato: magus (priest in some ancient eastern cultures, like Iranian/Zoroastrian)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek μάγος (mágos) (and perhaps partly through Old Church Slavonic магъ (magŭ)), from Ancient Greek μάγος (mágos). Also more recently borrowed in part from Latin magus, itself of the same Greek origin.
Borrowed from Greek μαγαζί (magazí), from Byzantine Greek μαγαζίον (magazíon), borrowed from Venetan magazén, borrowed from Arabic مَخَازِن (maḵāzin), from مَخْزَن (maḵzan), from خَزَنَ (ḵazana).
Borrowed from Greek μαϊμού (maïmoú) or Ottoman Turkish میمون (maymun), from Arabic مَيْمُون (maymūn), influenced by the suffix -uță.
Borrowed from Greek μαλακίων (malakíon). First attested in 1784.
Borrowed from Greek μάννα (mánna), partly through Bulgarian мана (mana). Cf. also Aromanian manã.
Borrowed from Greek μαραφέτι (maraféti), from Ottoman Turkish معرفت (marifet, marıfet), from Arabic مَعْرِفَة (maʕrifa).
Borrowed from Greek μαργιώλος (margiólos). Compare French mariole.
Borrowed from Greek μαρούλι (maroúli) (itself from Byzantine Greek μαρούλιον (maroúlion), from a derivative of Latin amarus) or Bulgarian маруля (marulja), and partly from Turkish marul.
Borrowed from Greek μασαλάς (masalás), from Ottoman Turkish مشعله (meşale), from Arabic مِشْعَل (mišʕal).
Borrowed from Greek μαυροφόρος (mavrofóros, “dressed in black”).
Borrowed from Greek μελωδία (melodía). First attested in 1704.

parole.significato: a piece of the wafer used in communion

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek μύδια (mýdia), plural of μύδι (mýdi, “mussel”). Compare Turkish midye.
Borrowed from Greek μίγμα (mígma) or Latin migma.
From Greek μύρισμα (mýrisma), via Bulgarian миризма́ (mirizmá). Compare Aromanian njurizmã, anjurizmã.

parole.significato: to become infected, to become contaminated
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek μόλεψα (mólepsa), aorist of μολύνω (molýno).
Borrowed from Greek μονέδα (monéda), from Venetan monéda, from Latin monēta; variant from Italian moneta. Compare Spanish moneda.
Borrowed from Greek μονομαχία (monomachía). By surface analysis, mono- + -mahie.
Borrowed from Greek μόστρα (móstra, “swatch, sample”), itself probably from Italian mostra (“show, sample”).
Borrowed from Greek μουτζουνάκι (moutzounáki), from μουτζούρα (moutzoúra).
Borrowed from Greek νεράντζι (nerántzi) or Bulgarian неранза (neranza).
Borrowed from Greek ναύαρχος (návarchos) or Latin navarchus.
Borrowed from Greek νευρικά (nevriká), from νευρικός (nevrikós).
Borrowed from Greek νόημα (nóima). Compare Aromanian noimã.

parole.significato: a collection of imperial Byzantine laws and church canons

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek ολιγάκη (oligáki), from ολίγος (olígos, “a little”).
Borrowed from Greek ορφανός (orfanós) or Late Latin orphanus. Largely replaced the older inherited oarfăn. Compare Aromanian oarfãn.
Borrowed from Greek ὀργανίζω (organízo). First attested in 1820.
Borrowed from Greek οβριός (ovriós), from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos).

parole.significato: volunteer in the 1821 Greek War of Independence

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek παντεσπάνι (pantespáni), from Ottoman Turkish پان دیسپانیا (pandispanya), from Italian pandispagna (“bread from Spain”).

parole.significato: ceremonious term to address a boyar
the counter where candles are sold in the church

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek πανικός (panikós) or French panique or Italian panico or German Panik.
Borrowed from Greek παπαγάλος (papagálos), from Italian pappagallo.
Borrowed from Greek παραπονῶ (paraponó). First attested in 1779.

parole.significato: to play a role in a thatre play
to abandon, to give up, to resign

parole.testo: From partidă, from Greek παρτίδα (partída), from Venetan partida.
Borrowed from Greek παρτίδα (partída), from Venetan partida.

parole.significato: church calendar for the calculation of Easter time

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek πασιέντζα (pasiéntza), from French patience.
Borrowed from Greek πάστα (pásta), from Italian pasta.

Often thought to be from Greek πάτος (pátos, “path”), but also possibly from Latin pactum (“fastened, fixed, planted”), with the loss of the -p- in the normal result, *papt, explicable through dissimilation from the initial consonant; compare păta, boteza.
Borrowed from Greek πατριώτης (patriótis) or French patriote or German Patriot.
Borrowed from Greek πεμπτουσία (pemptousía). First attested in 1792

parole.significato: a coin worth five para or five lei

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek πηχτή (pichtí), from πηκτή (piktí), ultimately from Persian پخته (pexte, “cooked”).

parole.significato: fiery (of or relating to fire, burning, and especially fireworks)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Greek πύρ (pýr), πύρος (pýros), potentially through Italian pirico.
Borrowed from Greek πυροστία (pyrostía) or Bulgarian пиростия (pirostija), from Greek πυρ (pyr, “fire”).
Borrowed from Greek έμπλαστρο (émplastro), Latin plastrum. Compare German Pflaster.
Borrowed from Greek πλίκος (plíkos), from Italian plico.
From Greek, compare πλήκτισα (plíktisa) or έπληξα (éplixa) (past of πλήττω (plítto)); probably from πληκτικός (pliktikós, “boring”) through the adjective plicticos.
Borrowed from Greek πληρεξουσιότητα (plirexousiótita). First attested in 1775.
Borrowed from Greek ποδάγρα (podágra). Compare Albanian podagër.
Borrowed from Greek πολιτεία (politeía), from Byzantine Greek πολιτεία (politeía).
Borrowed from Greek πορφύρα (porfýra). Doublet of purpură.
Borrowed from Greek πραγματεία (pragmateía). Doublet of pragmatic.
Borrowed from Greek πικραμύγδαλο (pikramýgdalo), from πικρός (pikrós, “bitter”) + μύγδαλο (mýgdalo, “almond”).

parole.significato: first rank in a noble hierarchy
The head of the monastic community of Mount Athos.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek πρώτη πεντάδα (próti pentáda).
Borrowed from Greek πρωτοδιάκονος (protodiákonos). By surface analysis, proto- + diacon.
Borrowed from Greek πρωτοσύγκελλος (protosýgkellos). By surface analysis, proto- + singhel.

parole.significato: Orthodox church music of chanting hymns

parole.testo: Unknown. Probably from Greek πούγγη (poúngi), πουγγί (poungí) Compare Aromanian pungã, punghe
Borrowed from Greek παπαδιά (papadiá, “the wife of a priest”). Compare Turkish papatya.

From Greek παστρεύω (pastrévo), possibly through a Bulgarian intermediate пастря (pastrja). Compare Albanian pastroj, Aromanian pãstrescu, spãstrescu. An alternate theory deriving it from Latin *parsitāre is unlikely.
Borrowed from Greek ρίγλα (rígla, “rule”), from Latin rēgula. Doublet of regulă.
Borrowed from Greek ρήγας (rígas), itself ultimately derived from Latin rex, regis. Doublet of rege. Cognate to Albanian rig.
Borrowed from Greek ρόμβος (rómvos) or French rhombe.
Borrowed from Greek σαλατιέρα (salatiéra), equivalent to salată + -ieră.
Borrowed from Greek σαλάτα f (saláta), ultimately from Latin salāta (“salted (thing)”), from salō (“to salt”), sal (“salt”). Compare Aromanian salatã.
Borrowed from Greek σιλτής (siltís), from Ottoman Turkish شلته (şilte), from Persian چلته (čelte).
Borrowed from Greek σάλτσα (sáltsa), from Italian salsa. Doublet of salsa.
Borrowed from Greek σαλαμούρα (salamoúra), ultimately from Late Latin salimuria.
Borrowed from Greek σαστίζω (sastízo), itself borrowed from Ottoman Turkish شاشمق (şaşmak).
Borrowed from Greek σκούφια (skoúfia), from Byzantine Greek σκούφια (skoúphia), from Italian scuffia.
Borrowed from Greek σκουλαμέντο (skoulaménto), from Italian scollamento.

parole.significato: drawer (open-topped box in a cabinet used for storing)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek σίγουρος (sígouros), from Venetan seguro, siguro, from Latin secūrus. First attested in the late 18th century.
Borrowed from Greek συλλάβισα (syllávisa), under the influence of silabă.
Borrowed from Greek συνοικέσιον (synoikésion). First attested in 1800.
Borrowed from Greek σώσω (sóso), future of σώνω (sóno). Already attested in the oldest texts.
Borrowed from Greek σπανάκι (spanáki), ultimately from Persian اسپناخ (espanâx).
Borrowed from Greek σπαράγγι (sparángi), from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).
Borrowed from Greek στακτή (staktí) or Old Church Slavonic стакти (stakti).

parole.significato: ghost, phantom, apparition, spectre, spook, shadow, shade, wraith

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek στρατοκρατία (stratokratía). By surface analysis, strato- + -crație.
Borrowed from Greek σύρμα (sýrma) or Ottoman Turkish صرمه (sırma).
Borrowed from Greek τάβλι (távli), from Latin tabula.
Borrowed from Greek θεοκάπηλος (theokápilos). First attested in 1858.
Borrowed from Greek θεοσέβεια (theoséveia). First attested in 1699.
Borrowed from Greek τιμόνι (timóni), from Venetan timón, from Late Latin tīmōnem, from Latin tēmōnem (“pole, beam”).
Borrowed from Greek τυραννικός (tyrannikós) or French tyrannique. By surface analysis, tiran + -ic.

parole.significato: title (prefix or suffix added to a name)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek τίτλος (títlos), from Latin titulus.
From Greek τόνος (tónos), probably originally a medical term in Romanian.
Borrowed from Greek τριαντάφυλλο (triantáfyllo). Compare Aromanian trandafilã, Albanian trëndafil, Ukrainian троянда (trojanda), Bulgarian трендафил (trendafil), Ladino trandafila.
Borrowed from Greek τριπόδι (tripódi). By surface analysis, tri- + -pod.

Possibly an expressive creation from early Romanian based on an onomatopoeic root tumb-, imitating the sound of a fall or abrupt jump (compare French tomber, Catalan and Portuguese tombar, Spanish tumbar, etc.), or alternatively from Greek τούμπα (toúmpa). Also found in Aromanian tumbã.
Borrowed from Greek τουρκομερίτης (tourkomerítis). By surface analysis, turc + -o- + merit.
Borrowed from Greek οίδημα (oídima). Compare Aromanian uimã.
Via Greek βανίλια (vanília) and Italian vaniglia, from Spanish vainilla.
Borrowed from Greek βάρβαρος (várvaros), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros). Doublet of barbar.

parole.significato: to candy (to have sugar crystals form in or on)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek ζάχαρη (záchari), borrowed from Byzantine Greek ζάχαρις (zákharis), from Ancient Greek σάκχαρις (sákkharis), from σάκχαρ (sákkhar), borrowed from Pali sakkharā, from Sanskrit शर्क॑रा (śárkarā), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *śárkaraH, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ćárkaraH, from Proto-Indo-Eu
Borrowed from Greek σκουρά (skourá), σκουριά (skouriá), from Ancient Greek σκωρία (skōría). See the doublets scoare (inherited from Latin) and scorie (borrowed from Latin and French).
Borrowed from Greek ζωγράφος (zográfos). Doublet of Zografi.
Borrowed from Greek ζαργάνα (zargána) or Ottoman Turkish زارغنه (zargana), from Greek σαργός (sargós), from Ancient Greek σαργός (sargós).

parole.significato: article of clothing; togs, clothes, toggery; especially that which is old and used
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek τσόλι (tsóli), τσούλι (tsoúli), from Ottoman Turkish چولا (çula, “sackcloth”).
